cards.prompt: After "Ready, set," a model gives these chances at temperature 1: **go 70%**, now 15%, then 10%, slow 5%. At which temperature is it **most likely** to pick "go"?

options.text: It's the same at every temperature

cards.explanation: A **low** temperature makes the top word even likelier, so at 0.2 it picks "go" almost every time. At 2, the chances even out and "go" is picked less often.

cards.prompt: A model gives the next word a **40%** chance. If it carries on from the same text **20** times, about how many times will it pick that word?
cards.explanation: 40% means about 4 times in every 10, so in 20 tries it's about **8** times. A chance is "how often", not "always".

cards.prompt: Which word is this model **most likely** to pick next?
cards.explanation: "Raining cats and **dogs**" is a common saying, so it's by far the most likely next word, even though it isn't what rain is made of. The model picks what usually comes next.

cards.prompt: A chatbot is writing a story about a dog. Early on, it happens to pick an unlikely word, and the dog is now **purple**. What happens to the rest of the story?

options.text: It carries on from "purple", so later words may follow on from it
It notices "purple" was unlikely and swaps it for a likelier word
It writes the rest as if "purple" had never been added
It throws the story away and starts again from the first word

cards.explanation: Once a word is added, it stays. The model reads **all** the text so far, "purple" included, and works out each next word from there, so one odd pick can steer the rest of the story. It never goes back to change a word.

cards.prompt: Would each job be better with a **low** temperature, or a **higher** one?

items.label: Writing code that has to work

cards.explanation: Code and facts have one right answer: **low**. Names and jokes want variety: **higher**.

cards.prompt: Why can a chatbot confidently name a book that doesn't exist?

options.text: Its temperature was set too low, so it couldn't pick the real book
It picks words that sound likely, not ones it has checked are true
It looked the book up online, but the page it found was out of date
It's trained to sound clever, so it makes things up on purpose

cards.explanation: A title, an author and a summary all **sound** likely, so the model writes them without checking they're true: a hallucination. A low temperature makes it more predictable, not more inventive, and a language model on its own doesn't look things up: it writes one likely word at a time.

cards.prompt: You're planning a holiday, and ask a chatbot when a museum is open.

steps.text: It says the museum opens on Mondays, and names the museum's website as its source. What do you do?

choices.text: Plan a Monday visit: it named a source
choices.consequence: Chatbots can invent sources, or name a real one and get the detail wrong. A source only helps if you open it.

choices.text: Open the museum's website and check the opening days
choices.consequence: Right: what the source really says is what counts.

choices.text: Ask the chatbot again, to see if it says Monday twice
choices.consequence: It can repeat the same mistake. Check outside the chatbot.

cards.explanation: Days, dates and sources are where hallucinations hide. **Open the source** (or find a trusted one) and check it really says what the chatbot claims.

cards.prompt: Match each situation to the idea it shows.

pairs.left: It learned from huge amounts of text which words come next
You turn a setting up to get wilder story ideas
It confidently names an author who never existed

cards.explanation: A **language model** learned from text which words come next; each possible next word gets a **chance**; **temperature** sets how adventurous its picks are; a **hallucination** is a confident false answer.
